Taxes and Price Ceilings

Put a tax on cigarettes and a cap on rent, then see who actually pays. A tax drives a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers get. The wedge lands heavier on the side that cannot walk away. A price ceiling freezes the price but makes buyers line up instead. The formula below splits the tax burden. For example, add a 100-won tax to one 🍬 candy. A 🧑 classmate who cannot live without candy pays almost all of the higher price. A classmate who can take it or leave it just stops buying. Then the 🏪 shop cuts its own price and shoulders the tax.

Pb=Ps+tP_b = P_s + tPb​=Ps​+t

Examples & Exercises

A tax of 333 is slapped on cigarettes. If demand is price-insensitive (Qd=10−0.5PQ_d = 10 - 0.5PQd​=10−0.5P), who mostly pays it?

Show proof
  1. The tax wedge is Pb=Ps+3P_b = P_s + 3Pb​=Ps​+3. Solving gives the seller's price Ps≈5.67P_s \approx 5.67Ps​≈5.67 and the buyer's price Pb≈8.67P_b \approx 8.67Pb​≈8.67.
  2. Against the pre-tax price 6.676.676.67, buyers pay 222 more and sellers receive 111 less — 67%67\%67% of the tax lands on consumers. The side that cannot walk away pays the tax.

A rent ceiling of 333 is imposed on a market whose equilibrium price is 555. What happens?

Show proof
  1. At the ceiling price 333, buyers want Qd=10−3=7Q_d = 10 - 3 = 7Qd​=10−3=7 while sellers offer only Qs=3Q_s = 3Qs​=3.
  2. The gap of 444 is the shortage. A policy meant to make things cheaper creates a queue of people who want to buy but cannot — the red dashed line in the picture is that boundary.
